title: Lantern and Regiment
premise: In the storm-wracked winter of 1871, Mirabel Vane keeps the Gannet Point light alone, grieving a spouse lost at sea and hiding their grief behind ledgers and lamp oil. When the army requisitions the town to stage an evacuation of the flooded coast, the regiment's ledger of names becomes the town's fate, and Mirabel — who knows every household by heart — is conscripted as the keeper of that ledger. Torn between the colonel who demands order, the fishermen who demand mercy, and the orphaned siblings who have quietly made a home in the lighthouse, Mirabel must decide who gets the last berth on the final evacuation boat. In the end, Mirabel surrenders the berth themselves, staying to keep the light for one last night, and finds that the family they feared they'd lost was the one that refused to leave without them.
about_author: Theo Sterling is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse logbooks and regimental requisition records along the northern coast. Their fiction is known for spare, salt-bleached prose and stories about the quiet people history forgets to name.

chapters.title: The Weight of Glass
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A routine night trimming the lamp establishes Gannet Point, the great storms, and Mirabel's grief for their late spouse, Ede. They polish the lens and speak to no one. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for peace, cracked when Mirabel catches themselves setting out two cups.

chapters.title: Names in the Log
chapters.summary: Mirabel records weather and passing ships in the lighthouse log, revealing their habit of noting small human details the official ledger forbids. A supply boat brings word of trouble down the coast. Beat: the comfort of routine, shadowed by the first mention of the rising water.

chapters.title: The Orphans at the Door
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Two siblings, Wren and Tam, half-drowned, arrive seeking shelter; their grandmother's cottage is gone. Mirabel takes them in 'for one night.' Beat: reluctant tenderness; the lighthouse feels less silent for the first time in a year.

chapters.title: One Night Becomes a Week
chapters.summary: Mirabel teaches Wren to trim wicks and Tam to coil line, telling themselves it's temporary. The town's fisherfolk begin leaving offerings at the lighthouse door. Beat: found family forming in small domestic rituals, which Mirabel refuses to name.

chapters.title: Red Coats in the Harbor
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Sergeant Hollis of the arriving regiment. The army requisitions Gannet Point to stage an evacuation of the flooded coast; the town's own ledger of households is confiscated. Beat: cold bureaucratic menace arriving in an otherwise warm world.

chapters.title: The Ledger with All the Names
chapters.summary: Mirabel is summoned to the customs house. The regiment's copy of the town ledger is water-damaged and incomplete; the colonel demands Mirabel, who 'knows everyone,' reconstruct it. Beat: dread — Mirabel's intimate knowledge is now a weapon pointed at their neighbors.

chapters.title: Colonel Ashworth's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth's POV. He explains the mathematics of the evacuation: one ship, fixed tonnage, a hard deadline before the next great storm. He values Mirabel's precision and distrusts their sympathy. Beat: the antagonist revealed as a man of terrible, reasonable logic.

chapters.title: Ink and Salt
chapters.summary: Mirabel begins rebuilding the ledger, and each name they write is a neighbor, a friend, a debtor, a grudge. Hollis observes, increasingly uneasy with his orders. Beat: the burden of authorship — writing a name may be deciding a life.

chapters.title: What Wren Saw from the Gallery
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. From the lamp gallery, Wren watches soldiers mark houses with chalk and sees her friend's family passed over. She begins sneaking into the customs house at night. Beat: the children are not bystanders; the stakes come home.

chapters.title: The Berth List
chapters.summary: Ashworth announces the evacuation will carry fewer souls than the town holds. A 'priority list' will decide berths: skilled trades, the young, the useful. Beat: open dread; the town turns on itself in the square.

chapters.title: Bread and Bitterness
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the baker's, neighbors who once left offerings now beg Mirabel to move names up the list. Old friend Marta Tull offers payment; old rival Cobb Fenwick offers threats. Beat: the cost of being trusted by everyone.

chapters.title: Tam's Silence
chapters.summary: Tam, who hasn't spoken since the flood took his grandmother, begins leaving folded paper boats on Mirabel's desk — each with a name inside. Beat: grief speaking sideways; Mirabel realizes the children fear being sent away and separated.

chapters.title: The Chalk Marks
chapters.summary: Hollis's POV. Chalked on doors: numbers of berths per household. Hollis watches a family erase their own mark and rewrite a smaller number to save a neighbor. Beat: his conscience cracks; he starts bending his reports.

chapters.title: A Storm in the Records
chapters.summary: A squall floods the customs house cellar; the original ledger is half-destroyed. Ashworth blames the town, suspects sabotage, and doubles the guard. Beat: rising tension — the document everyone's lives depend on is literally dissolving.

chapters.title: The Smuggler's Chart
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Old smuggler Brine Ollie reveals a second, unregistered boat — the Kestrel — that could carry forty more, if someone can crew and pilot her through the reef. Beat: a door of hope, with a price and a deadline.

chapters.title: Wren's Night Errand
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren breaks into the customs house to copy the berth list and is nearly caught by Hollis, who lets her go — and keeps her secret. Beat: unlikely alliance seeded; Wren learns her own family's names sit low on the list.

chapters.title: The Question at the Table
chapters.summary: Mirabel, Wren, and Tam confront it plainly: the lighthouse is 'essential' — one keeper may stay — but the children's names are on the boat list. Who goes, who stays, and who decides? Beat: the central choice made explicit and unbearable.

chapters.title: Ede's Coat
chapters.summary: Mirabel finds Ede's old sea coat and the unfinished letter Ede wrote before their last voyage. Flashback to their marriage and the promise: 'keep the light, and it keeps you.' Beat: grief fully surfaced; Mirabel understands why they've been hiding in duty.

chapters.title: Ashworth's Offer
chapters.summary: Ashworth, needing the reef passage surveyed, offers Mirabel a bargain: pilot the Kestrel's route and the children get guaranteed berths — on different ships. Beat: the devil's arithmetic; help offered only in a form that breaks the family apart.

chapters.title: The Town Meeting
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In the chapel, the town argues over the list: the young or the old, the skilled or the many. Marta proposes drawing lots; Cobb demands merit. Mirabel stays silent and is ashamed. Beat: community fracturing; Mirabel's silence as complicity.

chapters.title: Hollis's Report
chapters.summary: Hollis files a falsified report to buy the town three days, knowing discovery means a firing squad or worse. Beat: the sergeant becomes a quiet hero; the clock tightens — three days to the great storm.

chapters.title: Rehearsal at the Reef
chapters.summary: Mirabel, Brine Ollie, and Hollis sound the Kestrel's passage by night, using the lighthouse beam as a range marker. Beat: hope made practical; Mirabel realizes the light itself can be an instrument of rescue, not just routine.

chapters.title: Tam's Paper Fleet
chapters.summary: Tam finally speaks — one word, 'stay' — and reveals he has folded a paper boat for every name in the ledger, planning to float them so 'the sea gives them back.' Beat: the child articulates what the adults cannot; Mirabel weeps for the first time.

chapters.title: The List Is Sealed
chapters.summary: Ashworth seals the final berth list. Mirabel, holding the pen, must certify it as accurate. They sign — and privately resolve to act. Beat: point of no return; complicity transformed into conspiracy.

chapters.title: Cobb's Betrayal
chapters.summary: Cobb Fenwick, passed over for a berth, discovers the Kestrel plan and trades the secret to Ashworth for his family's places. Beat: betrayal born of fear, not evil; the plan is compromised.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Ashworth confronts Mirabel with evidence of the Kestrel scheme. Mirabel neither denies nor confesses, offering instead the truth of every name in the ledger. Beat: verbal duel; Ashworth wavers but places Mirabel under watch in the lighthouse.

chapters.title: Wren Steals the List
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Using Hollis's unwitting help, Wren copies the sealed berth list and distributes it through the town in one night — paper boats on every doorstep. Beat: the secret becomes the whole town's; collective courage ignites.

chapters.title: The Town That Would Not Be Numbered
chapters.summary: At dawn, the entire town appears at the harbor, refusing to board unless all board. Ashworth faces mutiny of a different kind. Beat: climax rising — moral force versus military order, the storm hours away.

chapters.title: Hollis's Choice
chapters.summary: Ordered to disperse the crowd, Hollis instead arrests his own commanding officer's authority with one act: he burns the duplicate list and declares the manifest illegible. Beat: sacrifice of the loyal soldier; the machinery of the requisition jams.

chapters.title: Ashworth Alone
chapters.summary: Ashworth's POV. Alone in the customs house, he rereads Mirabel's ledger with its human annotations and sees his own dead family in the margins. Beat: antagonist's humanity; he does not repent, but he hesitates — and hesitation is everything.

chapters.title: The Great Storm Arrives
chapters.summary: The storm hits early. The evacuation ship cannot hold station; the Kestrel must run the reef in the worst weather in a generation, guided by the Gannet Point light. Beat: nature strips away all arithmetic; only action remains.

chapters.title: Loading in the Dark
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In wind and blindness, the town loads both vessels. Mirabel carries Tam toward the Kestrel — and stops. Beat: the moment of choice arrives with no time to think, only to know.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: One place remains. Mirabel puts Wren in it, gives Tam to Marta's arms, and steps back onto the rocks. Beat: the title's promise kept — Mirabel chooses the light, the town, and the children's future over their own safety.

chapters.title: One Keeper, One Night
chapters.summary: Mirabel and Ashworth, stranded together, keep the lamp burning through the storm's worst hours so the boats can hold their bearings. They speak of Ede, of lists, of what a name is worth. Beat: climax of character — two keepers of different ledgers finding common ground in the dark.

chapters.title: Landfall
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The Kestrel makes the mainland; Wren organizes the landing with the authority of a girl who once stole a list. Beat: survival and agency; the children carry the story ashore.

chapters.title: The Morning After
chapters.summary: The storm passes. The relief ship arrives to find the lighthouse standing and Mirabel alive on the gallery, having kept the light all night. Ashworth, relieved of command, asks for nothing but a page of the ledger. Beat: exhaustion, grace, and quiet vindication.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The reconstructed ledger is entered into the official record, annotations and all. Names become history instead of arithmetic. Beat: memory honored; the theme of naming made explicit and earned.

chapters.title: Coming Home on the Tide
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the evacuated townsfolk return as the waters recede. Wren and Tam run up the lighthouse path. Marta reopens the bakery; even Cobb is met without hatred. Beat: belonging restored; the town rebuilt around what held it together.

chapters.title: Two Cups, Filled
chapters.summary: Mirabel sets out two cups again — and then two more. The lighthouse is no longer a tomb for grief but a home: Wren learning the lens, Tam folding boats with real names of the living. Beat: found family fully realized; grief integrated, not erased.

chapters.title: The Light Goes On
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Mirabel's POV. Mirabel adds a last line to the log — not weather, but names: those who stayed, those who returned, those who were saved. The lamp turns above the healed town. Beat: resolution and resonance — memory, belonging, and family kept burning like the light itself.
